video_title: Lawfare Daily: The New Command Economy with Kristen Eichensehr and Ashley Deeks
gist: Law professors Kristen Eichensehr and Ashley Deeks describe a 'new command economy' in which the US government uses equity stakes, export-license revenue shares, and enforcement and proxy roles to pull companies into national security policy, and they argue Congress should ban pay-to-play deals and require transparency.

insights.claim: The authors define a 'new command economy' as deeper US government involvement in corporations for national security: equity stakes, supply-chain focus, and using companies to enforce policy on others; they say it is deliberately provocative and not a claim that government runs the whole economy.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: Frames the regime as a continuum toward state capitalism, which sets how investors should price political and legal risk in strategic sectors.

insights.claim: Government intervention is clustered in semiconductors and critical minerals but is broadening to AI companies, advanced tech, firms with sensitive data, social media, and via tariffs a massive number of ordinary US companies.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: Exposure to government-directed deal-making is not limited to defense names; smaller non-obviously national-security firms can be pulled in.

insights.claim: Past US use of Defense Production Act-style seizure or mandated production was confined to wartime or severe crises such as the Korean War steel seizure; today it is used in peacetime with no end in sight.
insights.speaker: Ashley Deeks
insights.so_what: Peacetime permanence implies these interventions are a durable regime, not a temporary shock.

insights.claim: The Section 232 tariff tool has shifted from regulatory to transactional: tariffs on pharmaceuticals are used so companies commit to building US factories instead of simply paying duties.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
insights.so_what: Corporate capex commitments can become the price of tariff relief, so watch company announcements of US plants.

insights.claim: The authors argue the new command economy is not going away: supply-chain entanglement and frontline-enforcer roles have persisted across administrations of both parties.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: Treat the regime as bipartisan and persistent when assessing multi-year exposure.

themes.theme: Five corporate roles in national security

insights.claim: Companies are keys to national security supply chains, drawing government funding and ownership: CHIPS Act funding, critical-mineral investments at home and in allied countries, the Intel stake, and a golden share in US Steel.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: Strategic-sector firms may come with government as shareholder or funder, changing governance and capital allocation.

insights.claim: Companies are frontline enforcers or self-enforcers of export controls, tariff payments, and investment screening, modelled on banks enforcing sanctions after 9/11; failing at the role makes the firm itself an enforcement target.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: Compliance cost and enforcement risk are rising for a growing range of companies.

insights.claim: Companies serve as national security proxies, for example Oracle as the trusted security partner monitoring TikTok's compliance with the divestiture deal, including data flows to its Chinese parent and source-code changes.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: Oracle takes on an oversight role in the TikTok structure, with attached liability and political exposure.

insights.claim: The Trump administration uses US company products as diplomatic bargaining chips, reportedly including access to advanced NVIDIA chips offered to negotiating partners.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: Chip export access is a policy lever, so NVIDIA revenue can swing on diplomacy rather than demand.

insights.claim: Companies are used as sources of funds that government extracts in return for national security approvals: the Intel equity-for-grants swap, NVIDIA and AMD paying a share of China chip sales for export licenses, and about $10 billion in installments from TikTok US investors.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: China chip sales carry a government revenue share and regulatory-approval risk; approvals now have a price.
insights.quote: conditioning export licenses for Nvidia and AMD to sell their chips into China advanced chips into China on the companies paying the US government a percentage of their sales into China

insights.claim: Under the Intel deal, the company was to receive CHIPS grants as it built fabs but instead receives money in exchange for giving the government equity, a different kind of arrangement, as shown by documents made public in a shareholder lawsuit.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
insights.so_what: The Intel shareholder suit is a rare window into the terms and a possible legal catalyst.

insights.claim: These deals are hard to challenge: counterparties like Intel are unlikely to sue, third parties face standing problems, and few companies are willing to litigate, so little has reached court.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: Legality questions may stay unresolved for long periods, leaving structural policy risk in place.

insights.claim: Courts may defer less to the executive as national security claims become economic, because shareholder suits and Administrative Procedure Act process claims look like ordinary litigation and the concerns are less urgent than military ones.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: Judicial pushback is plausible in economic-security cases; watch the Intel shareholder suit.

insights.claim: The Anthropic supply-chain-risk designation litigation has run about six months; the speaker suspects Anthropic sued there because it could not wait, while not suing over earlier export controls, and notes courts may not keep pace with executive action.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
insights.so_what: Speed of government action versus courts means challenged firms bear interim damage.

insights.claim: Government is using national security framing in tech cases, such as arguing xAI's data center needed no Clean Air Act process and intervening in the OpenAI copyright case, so courts may treat AI differently from tariffs and equity deals.
insights.speaker: Ashley Deeks
insights.so_what: AI companies get national security carve-outs, a regulatory tailwind for AI infrastructure.

insights.claim: US courts have begun to rule against government sanctions when Americans are affected, for example enjoining sanctions on the International Criminal Court as applied to American law professors, suggesting more judicial scrutiny when the effects are domestic.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
insights.so_what: Domestic-impact framing is the most promising route to challenging economic security measures.

insights.claim: Intel's own SEC filings on the government stake list illegality among the risks to the deal, alongside shareholder concerns.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
insights.so_what: Legal-risk disclosure in filings is a signal to read for other government equity deals.

themes.theme: Public law values and conflict of interest

insights.claim: Government equity stakes create conflicts of interest and self-enrichment concerns when senior administration officials own or buy shares in companies receiving US investment.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: Raises political and reputational risk around stake-recipient companies.

insights.claim: The government as shareholder may distort its own decisions, for example authorizing more exports of a product it profits from than national security would justify, or pressure companies into business decisions that are not their best judgment.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: Government-owned names may see policy favoritism, and corporate strategy may be steered by political aims.

insights.claim: Government stakes in permit-heavy sectors like mining and nuclear may let regulators expedite permits for firms it owns while others wait.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
insights.so_what: Competitors without stakes may face slower permits; stakes could be a competitive advantage.

insights.claim: Using companies as agents creates principal-agent problems, driving both over-compliance (firms blocking adjacent transactions to avoid sanctions) and under-compliance (NVIDIA designing chips to skirt export rules, tariff underpayment).
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: Policy outcomes diverge from intent, so compliance behavior is a source of both risk and opportunity.

insights.claim: The US government has concealed specifics of some deals, including NVIDIA and TikTok, which undermines transparency and accountability.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: Undisclosed terms mean investors cannot fully price obligations.

insights.claim: The single biggest recommendation is for Congress to ban pay-to-play deals, limiting national security approvals or licenses to a filing fee and prohibiting officials from asking for or accepting payments.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: If enacted, revenue-share licensing for China chip sales would end.

insights.claim: Other recommendations: mandatory disclosure of investment agreements including private companies, a published economic security strategy with periodic review, report-and-wait provisions before stakes or proxy roles, ethics rules covering officials' adult children, and an Arms Export Control Act-style notification regime for high-end semiconductors.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: A notification regime for high-end chips would add a congressional approval step to chip exports.

insights.claim: Congress could reassert itself in a big way as it did after Watergate and Vietnam with the War Powers Resolution, IEEPA, and the National Emergencies Act, though the authors treat this as possible rather than likely.
insights.speaker: Ashley Deeks
insights.so_what: A legislative reset is a tail scenario for the current tariff and sanctions toolkit.

insights.claim: A company facing a government deal demand should remember the government is not its only audience: customers worldwide, other governments using similar tools, and public shareholders will react.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: Firms conceding to US demands carry reputational and foreign-government risk.

insights.claim: Foreign governments may object to US stakes in their companies; the US has bought shares in Australian and Canadian companies, and Brazil reportedly scrutinized a USA Rare Earth asset purchase that had US backing.
insights.speaker: Ashley Deeks
insights.so_what: US-backed critical-minerals deals abroad can meet host-country pushback.

insights.claim: The authors worry the regime will be judged on results such as investment returns or reduced rare-earth dependence on China, though profit does not mean values were respected, and there are less risky routes to the same goals.
insights.speaker: Kristen Eichensehr
insights.so_what: Early success could entrench the model, raising the likelihood of expansion.

insights.claim: Demand for lawyers in sanctions, tariffs, CFIUS, outbound investment review and export controls is growing, and in-house legal teams will face national security issues more often.
insights.speaker: Ashley Deeks
insights.so_what: Compliance spending in this area is likely to keep growing.
